phil:socrates: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher of the fifth century BC who left no writings of his own and is known chiefly through the dialogues of his student Plato and the accounts of Xenophon. He pioneered a method of persistent questioning, now called the Socratic method, that exposed the confusions and unexamined assumptions behind confident claims to knowledge, especially about virtue and justice. Insisting that the unexamined life is not worth living, he treated moral self-knowledge as the central task of philosophy. Tried on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth, he was condemned to death and drank hemlock, becoming an enduring emblem of intellectual integrity.
phil:plato: Plato was an Athenian philosopher of the fourth century BC, a student of Socrates and the founder of the Academy, one of the earliest institutions of higher learning in the Western world. Writing in dialogue form, he explored justice, knowledge, love, and the soul across works such as the Republic, the Symposium, and the Phaedo. He is best known for his theory of Forms, which holds that the changing things we perceive are imperfect copies of eternal, non-physical ideals grasped by reason rather than the senses. His thought shaped virtually every branch of later philosophy, prompting the remark that the tradition is a series of footnotes to Plato.
phil:aristotle: Aristotle was a fourth-century BC Greek philosopher who studied under Plato, tutored Alexander the Great, and founded his own school, the Lyceum. Rejecting Plato's separate realm of Forms, he located the essence of things within the things themselves and built a vast systematic account of the natural and human world across logic, biology, physics, ethics, and politics. He developed the first formal system of logic, argued that the good life consists in the exercise of virtue and reason, and analyzed causation, substance, and change in ways that framed inquiry for two millennia. His works became foundational to medieval Islamic, Jewish, and Christian thought and to the emergence of the sciences.
phil:heraclitus: Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher active around 500 BC in Ephesus, known for a deliberately obscure, aphoristic style that earned him the nickname the Riddler. He taught that reality is fundamentally in flux, captured in the idea that one cannot step into the same river twice, and that apparent stability masks ceaseless change. He held that this constant becoming is governed by an underlying rational principle, the logos, and that opposites are bound together in tension, as in his image of the harmony of the bow and the lyre. His emphasis on process and the unity of opposites influenced later dialectical thinking.
phil:parmenides: Parmenides was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of the early fifth century BC from Elea in southern Italy, and the central figure of the Eleatic school. In a philosophical poem, he argued that being simply is and that not-being cannot even be thought, concluding that reality is one, unchanging, and indivisible, while the world of motion and multiplicity revealed by the senses is mere appearance. This sharp division between the way of truth, reached by reason, and the way of opinion, tied to perception, posed a challenge that shaped subsequent metaphysics. His insistence that genuine knowledge comes through reason rather than the senses deeply influenced Plato.
phil:zeno-elea: Zeno of Elea was a fifth-century BC Greek philosopher and student of Parmenides, celebrated for a series of paradoxes designed to defend his teacher's claim that reality is single and unchanging. In arguments such as Achilles and the tortoise and the flying arrow, he tried to show that motion and plurality lead to contradiction and are therefore illusory. Whether or not his conclusions convince, his paradoxes sharpened questions about infinity, continuity, and the structure of space and time. Aristotle credited him with inventing dialectic, and his puzzles still occupy philosophers and mathematicians today.
phil:democritus: Democritus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of the fifth and fourth centuries BC who, with his teacher Leucippus, developed the ancient theory of atomism. He held that everything is composed of indivisible, indestructible particles called atoms moving through empty void, and that the qualities we perceive arise from their shapes, arrangements, and motions. On this view the world unfolds by mechanical necessity rather than design, an early materialist account of nature. Known as the laughing philosopher for his cheerful temperament, he also wrote on ethics, commending contentment and moderation.
phil:pythagoras: Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher and mathematician of the sixth century BC who founded a religious and philosophical community in southern Italy. He and his followers held that number is the underlying principle of reality and that the cosmos is ordered according to mathematical proportion, an idea reflected in their study of musical harmony and the heavens. The Pythagoreans also embraced doctrines such as the transmigration of souls and lived by strict communal rules. Because his teachings were transmitted through his school and shrouded in legend, it is often hard to separate the historical figure from later tradition, though his influence on mathematics and on Plato was profound.
phil:protagoras: Protagoras was a fifth-century BC Greek thinker and the most prominent of the Sophists, itinerant teachers who instructed the young in rhetoric and civic excellence for a fee. He is best known for the dictum that man is the measure of all things, an early statement of relativism suggesting that truth and value are relative to the individual perceiver rather than fixed and absolute. He also professed agnosticism about the gods, saying he could not know whether they exist. His views, sharply criticized by Plato, made him a central figure in ancient debates about knowledge, morality, and persuasion.
phil:diogenes-cynic: Diogenes of Sinope, known as Diogenes the Cynic, was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC and the most famous exponent of Cynicism. Rejecting wealth, convention, and social pretension, he lived in extreme poverty, reputedly making his home in a large ceramic jar, and used provocative acts and sharp wit to expose hypocrisy. He held that virtue is achieved by living simply and in accordance with nature, free from artificial desires and shame. The many anecdotes about him, including his search with a lantern for an honest man and his retort to Alexander the Great, made him a lasting symbol of defiant self-sufficiency.
phil:plutarch: Plutarch was a Greek philosopher, biographer, and essayist of the first and second centuries AD, writing under Roman rule and steeped in the Platonic tradition. He is best known for his Parallel Lives, which pair eminent Greeks and Romans to draw out moral character, and for the Moralia, a wide-ranging collection of essays on ethics, religion, and practical wisdom. More a moralist than a systematic theorist, he used history and biography to illuminate virtue and human conduct. His works profoundly shaped Renaissance and later European literature and thought.
phil:epicurus: Epicurus was a Greek philosopher of the fourth and third centuries BC who founded a school in Athens known as the Garden. Adapting the atomism of Democritus, he taught that the world consists of atoms and void and that fear of the gods and of death is unfounded, since the soul dissolves at death and the gods do not intervene in human affairs. He held that pleasure, properly understood as the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance, is the highest good, best attained through modest desires, friendship, and tranquil living. His ethics of serene contentment gave rise to the enduring, if often misunderstood, ideal of Epicureanism.
phil:pyrrho: Pyrrho of Elis was a Greek philosopher of the fourth and third centuries BC regarded as the founder of ancient skepticism, the tradition later named Pyrrhonism after him. He argued that because we cannot know the true nature of things, we should suspend judgment about all claims, neither affirming nor denying them. This suspension, he held, leads to tranquility of mind, or ataraxia, freeing one from the anxiety of dogmatic conviction. Leaving no writings, he is known through followers and later reports, most fully through Sextus Empiricus.
phil:sextus-empiricus: Sextus Empiricus was a Greek philosopher and physician of the second and third centuries AD and the chief surviving source for ancient skepticism. In works such as the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, he systematized the skeptical tradition, presenting sets of arguments, or modes, meant to induce suspension of judgment by balancing opposing claims against one another. He held that this suspension yields tranquility, and he carefully distinguished the skeptic's practical acceptance of appearances from any dogmatic assertion about hidden realities. Rediscovered in the Renaissance, his writings powerfully shaped early modern debates about knowledge and doubt.
phil:zeno-citium: Zeno of Citium was a Greek philosopher of the late fourth and early third centuries BC who founded Stoicism, teaching in Athens at the painted colonnade, or Stoa, from which the school takes its name. He held that the universe is governed by a rational order, or logos, and that living well means living in agreement with nature and reason. On this view virtue is the only true good, and emotional disturbances arise from mistaken judgments, so the wise person cultivates self-control and equanimity in the face of fortune. Though his own writings survive only in fragments, the philosophy he began became one of the most influential ethical systems of antiquity.
